title: No beings freed (section 25)
hook: the Tathagata doesn't think "I free beings"; there are no beings for him to free

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaps of jewels piled as high as mountains, and four lines kept by heart outweighed them all. Your line: less than four lines. Which four lines did you carry? Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

Two neighbors shovel the same snowy sidewalk for an old man down the street. One does it before dawn and never brings it up. The other does it and brings it up at every barbecue for a year. Same snow. Same shovel. Same clear path. But the second one carries something extra home: a little ledger. I did that. For him. He owes me. Section twenty-five of the Diamond Sutra goes after that ledger, and it goes after it at the very top. The Buddha asks Subhuti whether the Tathagata, the awakened one himself, ever thinks, I have set beings free. Today: no beings freed.
screen: `SAME SNOW, TWO SHOVELERS.` → `ONE KEEPS A LEDGER.` → `DOES THE BUDDHA KEEP ONE?`

segments.voice: First, the question. In section twenty-five the Buddha turns to Subhuti and asks, in paraphrase: what do you think? Does the Tathagata think, I have set beings free? And he answers his own question: don't think so, Subhuti. That's a strange thing to deny. The sutra itself opened with a vow to free all beings. Second, the reason. There is no being, the Buddha says, whom the Tathagata has set free. If he did think that way, he would be holding on to an idea of a self, a being, a living soul, a person: the same four ideas the sutra has been cutting since section three. Notice what goes and what stays. The help doesn't vanish. The helper's tally does. Third, a turn the sutra loves. What is called a self, the Buddha says, is taught by the Tathagata as no self, and yet ordinary, unlearned people hold on to it. Then he adds that those ordinary people are not ordinary people either; they are only called that. Nobody is written off as hopeless, not even the person still clinging. The label gets cut along with the self. Fourth, why it matters. Back in section three, the bodhisattva vowed to lead all beings to nirvana while knowing that no being is led. Section twenty-five turns that same vow around and points it at the Tathagata. Even at the very top, the rule holds. Some Mahayana teachers describe a gift as clean when the giver, the gift and the one who receives are all held lightly. A help that keeps no ledger has nothing to collect later, and nobody is left owing.
screen: `DOES HE THINK "I FREE BEINGS"?` · `NO BEING TO FREE.` · `SELF IS TAUGHT AS NO SELF.` · `HELP WITHOUT A LEDGER.` · then, large: `NO ONE TO FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: help someone and forget it. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Call to mind one small thing you could do for someone today: a text, a dish washed, a door held, a ride offered. Choose it. Now notice the little voice already taking notes: they'll appreciate that, they'll remember. Let that voice go quiet. See the help as just the next thing that needs doing, the way a hand brushes crumbs off a table. Then let the whole plan drop, and rest with the breath. When you do it later, do it and walk on. The bell holds the time.
No beings freed. Section twenty-five: the Tathagata doesn't think, I have set beings free, because there's no being he holds on to as freed. Today's word.
Your line: no one to free. Today, after one small kindness, walk on before anyone can thank you. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that study the Diamond Sutra, section 25 is read with the bodhisattva vow from section 3: beings are helped without the helper holding on to the thought "I freed them."

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: does the Tathagata think "I have set beings free"? what's the answer?
options: yes, that is his whole work
no: there is no being he has set free

fork.reveal: the Buddha says don't think so: if he held that thought, he'd be holding an idea of a self, a being, a soul, a person.

original.note: Sanskrit: a being, a living creature; the word inside bodhisattva, and the 'being' the Tathagata doesn't count as freed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha doesn't really free anyone.
what it means: he helps without the thought "I freed them," which would bring back a self, a being, a soul, a person.
what a scholar hears: section 25 turns the section 3 vow back on the Tathagata, and cuts the label 'ordinary people' too.

the line said to have woken Huineng

notes: Section 25 paraphrased, not quoted from Max Müller (wording unverified): check 'self taught as no self, yet held by ordinary/foolish people (balaprthagjana)' and 'ordinary people are not ordinary people, so called'.
'Some Mahayana teachers describe a gift as clean when giver, gift and receiver are held lightly' points at the 'threefold purity' teaching; confirm the fair description or cut.
'The Mahayana picture is of a Buddha who works for the freedom of beings' is a general description of the Mahayana Buddha ideal; soften if a Keeper prefers.
Editor: replaced the general 'Mahayana picture' claim with a pointer to the sutra's own section 3 vow; rewrote the carry, which echoed day 1136's 'tell no one, not even yourself later'.
